Klatt (1979, J Phon)
A very old and very general model of speech perception
On Monday, we discussed categorical 
perception.
The idea is that somewhere in the journey from 
the analog signal that comes in through the 
cochlea, and the activation of phonemes 
(segmental analysis), information is lost.  
This loss of information is helpful, because it 
allows us to make contact with higher levels of 
representation.
For example, we might assume that in order to 
identify words, we need to first identify their 
constituent phonemes.
Today we’ll talk about two problems for this 
simple view:
1. Cascaded processing, and
2. Feedback

A metaphor for thresholded activity: Making furniture.

A metaphor for thresholded activity: Making furniture.
The point is that each “layer” of the system can only take a specific input that’s been 
transformed completely by the previous layer. You have to wait for the shipment of lumber 
before you can start manufacturing, etc. 
(Many computer programs function this way.)

A metaphor for “cascaded” 
processing:
A “food web.”
“levels” continuously interact with 
one another, so that a drought 
reducing the number of plants will 
immediately have an impact on the 
health of kangaroo rats, which 
impacts the snakes, etc.
(Further, there are clear feedback 
loops in here…what impact does 
adding more hawks have on 
populations of snakes, lizards and 
rats?)

This finding is consistent with the idea that activation flows in a cascaded way from

Even stimuli that are identified as,

vary in how strongly and

If the stimulus is obviously

That ambiguity is reflected in eye-
movements while the participant 
decides where to click.

As the input unfolds over time, activity accumulates for “plug,” especially when the final /g/ 
arrives, which is highly inconsistent with “blood” and “blush” (also activated in Frame 3).
Thus, this model explains word effects on phoneme category boundaries in terms of top-
down processing. Specifically, activity from the lexical level can produces feedback to the 
phoneme level, producing greater activation for the phoneme consistent with a word.

This should remind you of something from a previous lecture!
In fact the TRACE model is a version of the Interactive Activation model for written word 
recognition.
Many of the principles are the same, but a key issue in speech perception is the way the 
stimuli unfold over time.

Categorical perception and the “lexical-phonetic interface”
As we saw last week, perception appears to be shaped by category boundaries.
Specifically: Given the same physical difference, it is more difficult to distinguish stimuli 
from the same category than from different categories.
Nothing we learned today really undermines that basic finding. 
BUT:
Ambiguity about phoneme identity does have an impact on word recognition. 
Word-level information seems to have an impact on phoneme categorization.
Thus, it can’t be the case that the word recognition system just sits there waiting for the 
phoneme recognition system to finish doing its job (like a lumber mill). Spoken word 
recognition seems to be more interactive than this.
